title: Logistic Regression
hook: Take linear regression, squash its output through a sigmoid, and you get a probability - turning a number-predictor into a classifier with one extra step.
key_points: Applies a sigmoid function to a linear weighted sum, converting it to a probability between 0 and 1.
Trained by maximizing likelihood (or minimizing cross-entropy loss), not least squares.
Output is a probability score, not just a hard label - useful for ranking and calibration.
It is literally a single neuron with a sigmoid activation - the atom of neural networks.
content_html: Logistic regression takes the same weighted sum of features as linear regression, but instead of outputting that number directly it passes it through a sigmoid function, which squashes any value into the range 0 to 1. That output is interpreted as the probability the input belongs to a certain class.
extra_html:
How it works

The sigmoid turns large positive values into probabilities near 1 and large negative values into probabilities near 0. Training finds the weights that make the true labels as probable as possible - a principle called maximum likelihood. Despite the word "regression" in its name, this is a classification algorithm.

Why it matters

Logistic regression is still a production workhorse for problems like spam detection and medical risk scoring because its outputs are well-calibrated probabilities and the model is easy to audit. It is also the conceptual bridge to neural networks: stack many logistic units and you have a multilayer perceptron. The Wikipedia article covers the math and the variants in depth.
